128f313b5 2009-11-17 jmaessen
[libraries, codegen] ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the
spec.  Over the next few weeks expect more coercions to come on line
as we gradually migrate to a flat numeric hierarchy.

This checkin in particular was a massive joint effort between myself
and the Austin folks (Eric, Justin, and Scott); everyone had their
fingers on most of the bits of code at some point in the past few
days.  And now it actually works!

====
116e5e6fa 2009-08-21 jmaessen
[compiler, library, tests] Work on getting RR64 to run
(seems OK so far except for the usual warts that also hold for ZZ32;
eg literals don't support asString due to dotted method inheritance
bugs).  Note that ZZ32 and RR64 arithmetic can't be commingled at all
at the moment.

Moved desugaring of loops and generalized if/while to occur before
type checking.  This makes these constructs work the same way as
comprehensions and reductions, which had previously been shifted
earlier in compilation.  Adjusted the desugarings to generate
_RewriteFnApp or MethodApplication nodes rather than TightJuxts.  This
should improve future reliability of desugared code.

Added test of floating-point printing.  Adjusted Compiled7fo to work
around obvious shortcomings in code generation.  Codegen now crashes
on this program, probably due to an outstanding bug that's been
lurking for a long time.  Addressing this is probably the next thing
to be done.

====
3e0306166 2009-10-16 sukyoungryu
[self-type idiom] Implemented the new self type.  Rewrote SelfParamDisambiguator in Scala.  Eliminated comprises clauses from ZZ32 and RR64.  Fixes here and there.  Added a test.

====
d0cde7d17 2010-01-13 EricAllen
Added coercions for RR32, RR64.

====
304f2743a 2012-06-12 Guy Steele
Made a patch for the MaybeTest15a bug; also implemented opr CHOOSE for ZZ, and getter asZZ for ZZ32, ZZ64, NN32, NN64, and coercions from those four types to ZZ; and wrote ChooseTest3

====

    10	%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
    11	
    12	\chapter{Numbers}
    13	\chaplabel{lib:numbers-basic}
    14	
    15	
    16	\section{Rational Numbers}
    17	\seclabel{basic-rationals}
    18	
    19	The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} (\STR{QQ}) encompasses all finite rational numbers,
    20	the results of dividing any integer by any nonzero integer.
    21	The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}star}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} with
    22	two extra elements, \EXP{+\infty} and \EXP{-\infty}.
    23	The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}splat}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} with
    24	one additional element, the indefinite rational (written \EXP{0/0}), which is used as the result
    25	of dividing zero by zero or of adding \EXP{-\infty} to \EXP{+\infty}.
    26	
    27	Often it is desirable to indicate that a variable ranges over only a subset of
    28	the rationals, such as only positive values or only nonnegative values or only
    29	nonzero values.
    30	Unfortunately, traditional notations such as \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^+} are not used consistently
    31	in the literature; one author may use \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^+} to mean the set of strictly positive rationals
    32	and another may use it to mean the set of nonnegative rationals.
    33	Fortress therefore uses a notation that is novel but unambiguous:
    34	
    35	\begin{tabbing}
    36	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} (\STR{QQ}) is the set of rationals
    37	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}).
    38	\\
    39	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{<}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}LT}) is the set of strictly negative rationals
    40	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\neq}}).
    41	\\
    42	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\leq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}LE}) is the set of nonpositive rationals, that is, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{<} \cup \{0\}}
    43	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}_{\leq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}).
    44	\\
    45	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\geq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}GE}) is the set of nonnegative rationals, that is, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{>} \cup \{0\}}
    46	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}_{\geq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}).
    47	\\
    48	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{>}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}GT}) is the set of strictly positive rationals
    49	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\neq}}).
    50	\\
    51	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\neq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}NE}) is the set of strictly nonzero rationals (that is, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{<} \cup \mathbb{Q}_{>}})
    52	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}_{\neq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\neq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}).
    53	\\
    54	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}star}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} with extra elements \EXP{+\infty} and \EXP{-\infty}
    55	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}}).
    56	\\
    57	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{<}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}star{\char'137}LT}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{<}} with extra element \EXP{-\infty}
    58	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^*_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\neq}}).
    59	\\
    60	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\leq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}star{\char'137}LE}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\leq}} with extra element \EXP{-\infty}
    61	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^*_{\leq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}).
    62	\\
    63	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\geq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}star{\char'137}GE}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\geq}} with extra element \EXP{+\infty}
    64	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^*_{\geq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}).
    65	\\
    66	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{>}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}star{\char'137}GT}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{>}} with extra element \EXP{+\infty}
    67	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^*_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\neq}}).
    68	\\
    69	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\neq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}star{\char'137}NE}) is
    70	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\neq}} with extra elements \EXP{+\infty} and \EXP{-\infty}
    71	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^*_{\neq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\neq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}).
    72	\\
    73	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}splat}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} with extra element \EXP{0/0}
    74	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^{\#}}).
    75	\\
    76	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{<}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}splat{\char'137}LT}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{<}} with extra element \EXP{0/0}
    77	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^{\#}_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\neq}}).
    78	\\
    79	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\leq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}splat{\char'137}LE}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\leq}} with extra element \EXP{0/0}
    80	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^{\#}_{\leq}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}}).
    81	\\
    82	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\geq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}splat{\char'137}GE}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\geq}} with extra element \EXP{0/0}
    83	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^{\#}_{\geq}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}}).
    84	\\
    85	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{>}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}splat{\char'137}GT}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{>}} with extra element \EXP{0/0}
    86	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^{\#}_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}},
    87	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\neq}}).
    88	\\
    89	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\neq}} (\STR{QQ{\char'137}splat{\char'137}NE}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\neq}} with extra element \EXP{0/0}
    90	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}^{\#}_{\neq}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}}).
    91	\end{tabbing}
    92	
    93	The Fortress type system tracks these types closely through various arithmetic
    94	operations; for example, adding two values of type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{>}} produces a result of type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{>}},
    95	and adding a value of type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{>}} and a value of type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\geq}} produces a value
    96	of type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\geq}}.
    97	
    98	Here we present only the trait \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and its methods.
    99	The other rational types have exactly the same methods and differ
   100	only in the details of the types of method arguments and results
   101	and exactly what traits are extended by each rational type.
   102	For example, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a field and is totally ordered,
   103	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} is totally ordered but is not a field,
   104	and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} is neither totally ordered nor a field.
   105	For the exact details of how all this is implemented, \see{advanced-rationals}.

    12	\section{Summations and Other Reduction Expressions}
    13	\seclabel{reduction-expr}
    14	
    15	\begin{Grammar}
    16	\emph{FlowExpr} &::=&
    17	\emph{Accumulator} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    18	\options{\texttt[ \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \texttt]} \emph{Expr} \\
    19	
    20	\emph{Accumulator} &::=& $\sum$ $|$ $\prod$ $|$ \KWD{BIG} (\emph{Encloser} $|$ \emph{Op})
    21	\end{Grammar}
    22	
    23	A \emph{reduction expression} begins with a big operator such as
    24	$\sum$ or $\prod$ followed by an optional static arguments and
    25	an optional generator clause list (described in
    26	\secref{generators}), followed by a body expression.
    27	There is no explicit relationship between \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} and
    28	\emph{Op}.  Instead, a reduction expression corresponds to a call to the
    29	\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} operator, which has the following header:
    30	%% opr BIG Op[\T\](g:(Reduction[\R0\],T->R0)->R0):R
    31	\begin{Fortress}
    32	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}}\: \emph{Op}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0})\COLONOP{}R\)
    33	\end{Fortress}
    34	Here \VAR{R} is the result type of the operator, and \VAR{g} corresponds to
    35	the method %generate[\R0\]
    36	\EXP{\VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket}
    37	of the trait %Generator[\T\]
    38	\EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}:
    39	it is a function that takes a reduction (of type %Reduction[\R0\]
    40	\EXP{\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket})
    41	and a body (of type \EXP{T\rightarrow{}R_{0}})
    42	and returns a value of type \EXP{R_{0}} by running body on each
    43	generated element and combining them using the reduction.
    44	When a generator clause
    45	list is provided, generator clauses produce values and bind the values to the
    46	identifiers that are used in the subexpression.  Each iteration of the
    47	body expression is assumed to be evaluated in a separate implicit
    48	thread as described in \secref{generators}.  The resulting values are
    49	combined together using \emph{Op}
    50	\label{redexpr-redvar}
    51	as with reduction variables (see \secref{reduction-vars}).
    52	The value of a reduction expression is this combined value.
    53	When no generator clause list is provided, the body is taken to be an
    54	object of type \TYP{Generator} and the elements it generates are
    55	combined.  Thus, the reduction expression \EXP{\sum a} is equivalent
    56	to \EXP{\sum\limits_{x\leftarrow{}a}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu{x}}.
    57	
    58	A reduction expression with a generator list:
    59	%% \sum [v_1 \gets g_1, v_2 \gets g_2, \ldots] e
    60	\begin{Fortress}
    61	\(\sum [v_{\mathrm{1}} \gets g_{\mathrm{1}}, v_{\mathrm{2}} \gets g_{\mathrm{2}}, \ldots] e\)
    62	\end{Fortress}
    63	is equivalent to the following code:
    64	%do
    65	%  var result: ZZ32 = 0
    66	%  for v1 <- g1, v2 <- g2, \ldots do
    67	%    result += e
    68	%  end
    69	%  result
    70	%end
    71	\begin{Fortress}
    72	\(\KWD{do}\)\\
    73	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{var}\:\VAR{result}\COLON \mathbb{Z}32 = 0\)\\
    74	\(  \KWD{for}\:v_{1} \leftarrow g_{1}, v_{2} \leftarrow g_{2}, \ldots \KWD{do}\)\\
    75	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{result} \mathrel{+}= e\)\-\\\poptabs
    76	\(  \KWD{end}\)\\
    77	\(  \VAR{result}\)\-\\\poptabs
    78	\(\KWD{end}\)
    79	\end{Fortress}
    80	where \VAR{result} is a fresh variable.
    81	%
    82	A reduction expression without a generator clause list:
    83	%% \sum g
    84	\begin{Fortress}
    85	\(\sum g\)
    86	\end{Fortress}
    87	is equivalent to the following:
    88	%\sum [x \gets g] x
    89	\begin{Fortress}
    90	\(\sum [x \gets g] x\)
    91	\end{Fortress}
    92	Note that reduction expressions without generator clause lists can be used to
    93	conveniently sum any aggregate expression (described in
    94	\secref{aggregate-expr}), since every aggregate expression
    95	is a generator.
    96

114	\section{Big Operator Declarations}
115	\seclabel{big-operators-impl}
116	
117	A \emph{big operator} such as $\sum$ or $\prod$ is declared as a usual
118	operator declaration.
119	See \secref{defining-generators} for an example declaration of a big operator.

122	described in \secref{comprehensions}.

     9	%
    10	%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
    11	
    12	\subsection{Reduction Variables}
    13	\seclabel{reduction-vars}
    14	
    15	\note{Reduction variables are not yet supported.}
    16	
    17	To perform computations as locally as possible, and avoid the need to
    18	synchronize in the middle of relatively simple \KWD{for} loops,
    19	Fortress gives special treatment to \emph{reductions}.  We say that an
    20	operator \EXP{\odot} is a \emph{reduction operator} for type $T$ if
    21	$T$ is a subtype of
    22	%Monoid[\T, ODOT\]
    23	\(\TYP{Monoid}\llbracket{}T, \odot\rrbracket\), which implies that
    24	\EXP{\odot} is an associative binary infix operator on $T$ (see
    25	\secref{monoids-groups-rings-fields} for details about the
    26	\TYP{Monoid} trait).
    27	
    28	We say that a variable \VAR{l} is a \emph{reduction variable} reduced using
    29	the reduction operator $\odot$ for a particular thread group if it
    30	satisfies the following conditions:
    31	\begin{itemize}
    32	\item Every assignment to \VAR{l} within the thread group is of the
    33	  form \EXP{l \mathrel{\oplus}= e}, where exactly one operator $\oplus$ or its
    34	  group inverse $\ominus$ (see below) is used in these assignments.
    35	\item The value of \VAR{l} is not otherwise read within the thread group.
    36	\item The variable \VAR{l} is not a free variable of a functional.
    37	  This includes the fields of the receiver object in a method
    38	  definition.
    39	\end{itemize}
    40	Other threads which simultaneously reference a reduction variable
    41	while a loop is running may see an arbitrary value for that variable.
    42	Any updates performed by those threads may be lost.  The association
    43	of terms in the reduction is arbitrary and guided by the loop
    44	generators (\secref{defining-generators}).  The order of terms in the
    45	reduction is the natural order of elements in the generator.  When the
    46	operator is commutative, the order of terms is also arbitrary.
    47	
    48	Several common mathematical operators are declared to be monoids in
    49	\library.  These include \EXP{+}, $\cdot$, \EXP{\wedge}, \EXP{\vee},
    50	and \EXP{\xor}.  If a type $T$ extends
    51	%Group[\T, OPLUS, OMINUS\]
    52	\EXP{\TYP{Group}\llbracket{}T, \oplus, \ominus\rrbracket}
    53	(see \secref{monoids-groups-rings-fields} for details about the
    54	\TYP{Group} trait)
    55	then reduction expressions of the following form are also permitted:
    56	%x OMINUS= y
    57	\begin{Fortress}
    58	\(x \mathrel{\ominus}= y\)
    59	\end{Fortress}
    60	Such expressions may be transformed into an algebraic equivalent such
    61	as the following:
    62	%x OPLUS= Identity[\OPLUS\] OMINUS y
    63	\begin{Fortress}
    64	\(x \mathrel{\oplus}= \TYP{Identity}\llbracket\oplus\rrbracket \ominus y\)
    65	\end{Fortress}
    66	
    67	The semantics of reductions enables implementation strategies such as
    68	the one used in OpenMP~\cite{OpenMP}: A reduction variable \VAR{l} is
    69	assigned \EXP{\TYP{Identity}\llbracket\oplus\rrbracket}
    70	at the beginning of each iteration.  The
    71	original variable value may be read ahead of time, resulting in the
    72	loss of parallel updates to the variable which occur in other threads
    73	while the loop is running.  When all iterations are complete, the
    74	initial value of the reduction variable and values of the variable at
    75	the end of each implicit thread are reduced and the result is assigned
    76	to the reduction variable as the group completes.
    77	
    78	In the following example, \VAR{sum} is a reduction variable:
    79	\note{I manually rendered the array type.}
    80	%arraySum[\nat x\](a:ZZ64[x]):ZZ64 = do
    81	%    sum:ZZ64 := 0
    82	%    for i<-a.indices do
    83	%        sum+=a[i]
    84	%    end
    85	%    sum
    86	%end
    87	\begin{Fortress}
    88	\(\VAR{arraySum}\llbracket\KWD{nat}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu{x}\rrbracket(a\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64[x])\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 = \;\KWD{do}\)\\
    89	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{sum}\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64 \ASSIGN 0\)\\
    90	\(    \KWD{for}  \null\)\pushtabs\=\+\(i\leftarrow{}a.\VAR{indices} \KWD{do}\)\\
    91	\(        \VAR{sum}\mathrel{+}=a[i]\)\-\\\poptabs
    92	\(    \KWD{end}\)\\
    93	\(    \VAR{sum}\)\-\\\poptabs
    94	\(\KWD{end}\)
    95	\end{Fortress}
    96	
    97	The following demonstrates the use of a reduction variable \VAR{prod}
    98	in a parallel \KWD{do}:
    99	\note{The $\mathrel{\cdot}$ is manually edited.}
   100	%prod : ZZ64 := 1
   101	%do
   102	%    prod DOT= g(y)
   103	%also do
   104	%    prod DOT= f(x)
   105	%    prod DOT= g(x)
   106	%also do
   107	%    h(x,y)
   108	%end
   109	\begin{Fortress}
   110	\(\VAR{prod} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\mathbb{Z}64 \ASSIGN 1\)\\
   111	\(\KWD{do}\)\\
   112	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{prod} \mathrel{\cdot}= g(y)\)\-\\\poptabs
   113	\(\KWD{also}\;\;\KWD{do}\)\\
   114	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{prod} \mathrel{\cdot}= f(x)\)\\
   115	\(    \VAR{prod} \mathrel{\cdot}= g(x)\)\-\\\poptabs
   116	\(\KWD{also}\;\;\KWD{do}\)\\
   117	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    h(x,y)\)\-\\\poptabs
   118	\(\KWD{end}\)
   119	\end{Fortress}
   120	
   121	The operator associated with a reduction variable can be invoked in
   122	several places during evaluation of a thread group.  Most obviously,
   123	it can be invoked anywhere the reduction operation occurs textually in
   124	the code for that group.  The operator can also be invoked multiple
   125	times implicitly and in parallel after the completion of some or all
   126	of the threads in the group.  The group as a whole does not complete
   127	normally until all these operator invocations have completed normally
   128	and the reduced result has been assigned to the reduction variable for
   129	use in subsequent computation.  If any operator invocation completes
   130	abruptly, it is treated just as if an ordinary implicit thread in the
   131	group completed abruptly.

strToInt(s: String, radix: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
    if |s| = 0 then fail("strToInt of empty string") end
    (i0, neg) =
        if s[0] = '-' then (1, true)

    n = |s| - 1

(* Q1SumWalk -- what SUM, PROD and the big MAX/MIN return today on the
   interpreter, for each element type and for the empty reduction: the value
   and its run-time type (ilkName).  One line per case. *)
component Q1SumWalk
export Executable

show(tag: String, x: Any): () = println(tag ": " x " : " (typecase x of o: Object => o.ilkName else => "?" end))

(* the shape of MicroGptFlat.fss:69 (matOffset) with a declared ZZ32 result *)
offs(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = SUM[j <- 0#i] (3 j)
(* the same with a declared RR64 result *)
rsum(i: ZZ32): RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#i] (1.5 j)

run(): () = do
    show("SUM ZZ32 empty    SUM[j <- 0#0] j", SUM[j <- 0#0] j)
    show("SUM ZZ32          SUM[j <- 0#4] j", SUM[j <- 0#4] j)
    show("SUM RR64          SUM[j <- 0#4] (0.5 j)", SUM[j <- 0#4] (0.5 j))
    show("SUM ZZ64          SUM[j <- 0#4] widen(j)", SUM[j <- 0#4] widen(j))
    show("SUM ZZ big        SUM[j <- 0#4] big(widen(j))", SUM[j <- 0#4] big(widen(j)))
    show("SUM QQ            SUM[j <- 1#3] (big(widen(1)) / big(widen(j)))", SUM[j <- 1#3] (big(widen(1)) / big(widen(j))))
    show("SUM mixed         SUM[j <- 0#2] (if j = 0 then 1 else 0.5 end)", SUM[j <- 0#2] (if j = 0 then 1 else 0.5 end))
    a0 = array[\RR64\](0)
    show("SUM RR64 empty    SUM a0 (0 elements)", SUM a0)
    a3 = array[\RR64\](3).fill(fn (i: ZZ32): RR64 => 0.25 + i)
    show("SUM RR64 array    SUM a3", SUM a3)
    show("SUM ZZ32 overflow SUM[j <- 0#2] 2147483647", SUM[j <- 0#2] 2147483647)
    show("offs(0): ZZ32     (matOffset shape, empty)", offs(0))
    show("offs(3): ZZ32", offs(3))
    show("rsum(0): RR64     (declared RR64, empty)", rsum(0))
    show("PROD ZZ32 empty   PROD[j <- 1#0] j", PROD[j <- 1#0] j)
    show("PROD ZZ32         PROD[j <- 1#4] j", PROD[j <- 1#4] j)
    show("PROD RR64         PROD[j <- 1#3] (0.5 j)", PROD[j <- 1#3] (0.5 j))
    show("BIG MAX RR64      BIG MAX a3", BIG MAX a3)
    show("BIG MAX ZZ32      BIG MAX[j <- 0#4] j", BIG MAX[j <- 0#4] j)
    show("BIG MAXN empty    BIG MAXN[j <- 0#0] j", BIG MAXN[j <- 0#0] j)
    show("BIG MINN ZZ32     BIG MINN[j <- 0#4] j", BIG MINN[j <- 0#4] j)
    show("x / SUM (sm shape) a3 / (SUM a3) elt 0", (a3[0]) / (SUM a3))
    show("BIG MAX empty     BIG MAX a0 (expect EmptyReduction)",
         try BIG MAX a0 catch e Exception => "threw " e.ilkName end)
  end
end

component fact64
export Executable

(* Computing factorial, in 64 bits.  Notice the call to "widen";
   this is necessary at least with the current interpreter, which 
   otherwise cheerfully multiplies two 32-bit integers giving a 32-bit
   result, in a way that would not surprise Kernighan and Ritchie

1	
     2	\chapter{Conversions and Coercions}
     3	\chaplabel{conversions-coercions}
     4	
     5	\note{Widening and where clauses are not yet supported.
     6	
     7	The examples in this chapter are not tested nor run by the interpreter.}
     8	
     9	\note{
    10	\begin{itemize}
    11	 \item ``has a type'' vs ``is a subtype of the type or could be coerced to the type''
    12	\item Coercion between tuple types (Victor's email titled ``Coercion between tuple types'' on 07/16/07) and arrow types
    13	
    14	\item Vectors and matrices: \secref{aggregate-expr}
    15	
    16	\item Do we allow coercion declarations in object expressions?
    17	
    18	\item If tests and coercion
    19	
    20	Suppose a test in an expression has a type that is not \TYP{Boolean}
    21	(or a subtype of \TYP{Boolean}) but is coercible to \TYP{Boolean}.
    22	Presumably, that is not a static error? But note that F1.0 beta
    23	makes no mention of this case; all tests in an if expression must be of
    24	type \TYP{Boolean}. There are similar problems with other expression types;
    25	we need to revisit them all in light of the coercion facility...
    26	
    27	\end{itemize}
    28	}
    29	
    30	Fortress provides a mechanism, called \emph{coercion}, to allow a
    31	value of one type to be automatically converted to a value of another
    32	type.  Programmers can define coercions (described in
    33	\secref{coercion-declarations}) and coercions may change the set of
    34	applicable declarations for a call (as described in
    35	\secref{applicability-with-coercion}).  If multiple coercions can be
    36	applied to a particular functional call then the most appropriate
    37	coercion is chosen statically.  Restrictions on coercion declarations
    38	(described in \secref{restrictions-coercion}) guarantee that the
    39	static resolution of coercion (described in
    40	\secref{resolving-coercion}) is well-defined.  Fortress provides
    41	implicit coercions for tuple types and arrow types (described in
    42	\secref{coercion-tuple-arrow}).  Fortress also provides an additional
    43	feature of coercion that allows ``widest-need'' evaluation of
    44	numerical expressions (described in \secref{widening}).
    45	
    46	\section{Principles of Coercion}
    47	\seclabel{coercion}
    48	
    49	In certain situations it is convenient to be able to use a value of
    50	one type \VAR{T} as if it were a value of another type \VAR{U} even
    51	though \VAR{T} is not a subtype of \VAR{U}.  For example, it is
    52	convenient to be able to use an integer-valued expression
    53	in a floating-point expression even though its
    54	type is not a subtype of any floating-point type.  Fortress supports
    55	the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point values (the
    56	technical term for this kind of automatic conversion is coercion).  In
    57	this way one can write \EXP{(x + 1)/2} rather than \EXP{(x +
    58	1.0)/2.0}, for example.  Such coercion applies generally to function
    59	and method (collectively called as functional) calls as well as to
    60	operators; one can write \EXP{\ln 2} rather than \EXP{\ln 2.0}, or
    61	\EXP{\arctan(1,1)} rather than \EXP{\arctan(1.0,1.0)}, for example.
    62	
    63	One way to think about coercion is that if type \VAR{T} can be coerced
    64	to type \VAR{U}, then a value of type \VAR{T} can be used to ``stand
    65	in'' for a value of type \VAR{U} in a functional call, for example.  This is
    66	different from actually \emph{being} of type \VAR{U}; it means only
    67	that, given any value of type \VAR{T}, an appropriate value of type
    68	\VAR{U} can be computed to substitute for it.  Also, coercion occurs
    69	only when the declared type of the corresponding parameter in the
    70	functional declaration is exactly the type \VAR{U} being coerced to
    71	 not if it is a supertype of \VAR{U}.  Note, however, that if type
    72	 \VAR{T} can be coerced to type \VAR{U} then any subtype of \VAR{T}
    73	 can also be coerced to type \VAR{U}.
    74	
    75	Coercion from \VAR{T} to \VAR{U} may occur in an expression context
    76	where the context expects the expression to have type \VAR{U} and
    77	the type of the expression is a subtype of \VAR{T} except for the following
    78	cases:
    79	\begin{itemize}
    80	\item type ascriptions (see \secref{type-ascription})
    81	\item type assumptions (see \secref{type-assumption})
    82	\end{itemize}
    83	For example, a coercion may occur in a variable definition when the
    84	declared type of the variable is \VAR{U} and the type of the expression on
    85	the right-hand side is a subtype of \VAR{T}.
    86	
    87	
    88	The expression contexts where a coercion can occur are:
    89	\begin{itemize}
    90	\item the right-hand sides of variable and field declarations where the
    91	  left-hand sides have declared types
    92	\item arguments to functionals and constructors where the corresponding
    93	  parameters have declared types
    94	\item body expressions of functionals and constructors where the return
    95	  types are declared
    96	\item the right-hand sides of test and property declarations
    97	\item expressions in contracts
    98	\item expressions whose enclosing expressions constrain the types of
    99	  their subexpressions
   100	\end{itemize}
   101	\chapref{expressions} describes the type constraints for each expression in
   102	Fortress.
   103	
   104	\note{
   105	  \begin{itemize}
   106	\item assignment expressions with type on the left-hand sides
   107	\item filter in a generator
   108	\item spawn
   109	\item throw
   110	\item while Expr
   111	\item if Expr
   112	\item if . then Expr end
   113	\item at Expr
   114	  \end{itemize}
   115	}
   116	
   117	Coercion is \emph{not} automatically chained in Fortress, unlike some
   118	other programming languages: even if type \VAR{T} can be coerced to
   119	type \VAR{U} and type \VAR{U} can be coerced to type \VAR{V}, it is
   120	not necessarily the case that type \VAR{T} can be coerced to type
   121	\VAR{V}.  Type \VAR{T} can be coerced to type \VAR{V} only if this
   122	coercion is explicitly defined.
   123	
   124	The basic principles behind coercion are (1) a decision by the
   125	designer of a trait \VAR{U} that, in all circumstances where a
   126	functional is to be called, an actual argument of some other type
   127	\VAR{T} may be used to satisfy a parameter of type
   128	\VAR{T}, and (2) a language mechanism for putting this decision into
   129	effect automatically and concisely.
   130	
   131	Example 1: For any floating-point parameter, a decimal integer literal
   132	argument may be used.
   133	
   134	Example 2: For any floating-point parameter, a floating-point argument
   135	of a shorter format may be used.
   136	
   137	Example 3: For any floating-point interval parameter, a non-interval
   138	floating-point argument (of the same or shorter floating-point format) may be used.
   139	
   140

Example 1: For any floating-point parameter, a decimal integer literal
argument may be used.

Example 2: For any floating-point parameter, a floating-point argument
of a shorter format may be used.

Example 3: For any floating-point interval parameter, a non-interval
floating-point argument (of the same or shorter floating-point format) may be used.



\section{Coercion Declarations}
\seclabel{coercion-declarations}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{Coercion} &::=&
\KWD{coerce}\option{\emph{StaticParams}}\texttt(\emph{BindId} \emph{IsType}\texttt)\emph{CoercionClauses} \option{\KWD{widens}} \EXP{=} \emph{Expr}\\

\emph{CoercionClauses} &::=&
\option{\emph{CoercionWhere}}
....
\seclabel{applicability-with-coercion}

As discussed in the previous section, coercion in Fortress alters the
set of applicable declarations for a particular functional call.  In
this section we formally define the applicability of declarations with
coercion.  (This level of formality is necessary to discuss the
interaction of overloading and coercion.)
We build on the terminology and notation defined in
\chapref{multiple-dispatch}.

A \emph{coercion} from $T$ to $U$ is defined in the declaration of $U$.
We write $T \coercedefto U$ if $U$ defines a coercion from $T$.
We say that $T$ \emph{can be coerced to} $U$, and we write $T \coercesto
U$, if $U$ defines a coercion from $T$ or any supertype of $T$; that
is, $T \coercesto U \iff \exists T': T \Ovrsubtype T' \logicand T'
\coercedefto U$.

We define coercion between tuple types and arrow types in
\secref{coercion-tuple-arrow}.

Because of automatic coercion, a declaration may be applicable even if
its parameter type is not a supertype of the argument type of the
call.  We define a new relation, \emph{substitutability}, that takes
coercion into account.

We say that a type $T$ is \emph{substitutable} for type $U$, and we
write $T \substitutable U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ can be
coerced to $U$; that is,
\[
T \substitutable U \iff T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor T \coercesto U.
\]

Note that $\substitutable$ need not be transitive.  This is a result
of the fact that coercion does not chain.
However, if $T$ is substitutable for $U$ then so are $T$'s subtypes;
that is, $A \Ovrsubtype T \logicand T \substitutable U \implies A
\substitutable U$.

A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{applicable with coercion} to a
call $\f(\Cs)$ if the call is in the scope of the declaration and
$\Cs \substitutable \Ps$.
(See \chapref{names} for the definition of scope.)

Recall a rewriting of
named functional calls into dotted method calls when no declarations
are applicable to the named functional call.  This rewriting is also
used to determine applicability with coercion.  If there is no
declaration applicable with coercion to a named functional call then
the call is rewritten into a dotted method call.
Applicable declarations are then
determined by the rules for applicability with coercion for dotted
method calls.

Similarly, a dotted method declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is
\emph{applicable with coercion} to a dotted method call
$\Cs_0.\f(\Cs)$ if it $\Cs_0 \Ovrsubtype \Ps_0$ and $\Cs
\substitutable \Ps$.  Notice that the receiver is compared using the
subtype relation instead of the substitutable relation.  This reflects
the restriction that receivers of dotted methods cannot be
coerced.  However, \KWD{self} parameters of functional methods can be
coerced.  This distinction is consistent with the intuition that
functional methods are rewritten into top-level functions.

Note that the only difference between applicability and applicability
with coercion is that substitutability is used instead of subtyping
to compare the parameter types of the declarations.

Also note that the definition of applicability with coercion does not
take keyword parameters or varargs parameters into account.  Such
declarations are conceptually rewritten into numerous declarations
which cannot be called with elided arguments nor with variable number of
arguments (as described in \secref{applicability-with-special-params}).  If
one of the expanded declarations is applicable with coercion to a call,
then the original declaration (with keyword or varargs parameters) is
applicable with coercion to the call.



\section{Coercion Resolution}
\seclabel{resolving-coercion}
For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a
declaration that is applicable without coercion.  If so, the most
specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are
explicitly added to the functional call.  If more than one coercion is
possible then the coercion that yields the most specific type is
chosen.  \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} describe overloading rules for the
declarations of coercions and overloaded functionals that guarantee
there exists always a most specific coercion when two or more are possible.

We first define a notion of more specific types in the presence of coercion.
Recall from \secref{type-relations} that Fortress defines an
\emph{exclusion} relation between types which is denoted by $\excludes$.

For types $T$ and $U$, we say that $T$ \emph{rejects} $U$,
and write $T \rejects U$, if for all coercions to $T$, the type coerced

input.description: Read spec coercion resolution rules

content.content:
and write $T \rejects U$, if for all coercions to $T$, the type coerced
from excludes $U$:
\[
T \rejects U \iff \forall A: A \coercedefto T \implies A \excludes U.
\]
Note that $T \rejects U$ implies $U \not\coercesto T$.

We say that $T$ is \emph{no less specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecificeq U$, if $T$ is a subtype of $U$ or $T$ excludes, can be
coerced to, and rejects $U$:
\[
T \morespecificeq U \iff
T \Ovrsubtype U \logicor
(T \excludes U \logicand T \coercesto U \logicand T \rejects U).
\]

The $\morespecificeq$ relation is reflexive and antisymmetric but not
necessarily transitive.  It is possible, for example, for
three types, $T$, $U$ and $V$, each excluding the other two,
to have coercions from $T$ to $U$ and from $U$ to $V$.  In
this case, $T \morespecificeq U$ and $U \morespecificeq V$ but
$T \not\morespecificeq V$.

Notice that if two tuple types have a bijective correspondence
between their element types then the $\morespecificeq$ relationship between
the tuple types is equivalent to applying the $\morespecificeq$
relation elementwise.

We say that $T$ is \emph{more specific} than $U$, and write $T
\morespecific U$, if $T \morespecificeq U \logicand T \neq U$.

We extend the definitions of no less specific and more specific to
declarations.  We say that a declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecificeq \Qs$.
Similarly, we say that a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{no less
specific} than a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps)
\morespecificeq (\Qs_0, \Qs)$.  A declaration $\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more
specific} than a declaration $\f(\Qs)$ if $\Ps \morespecific \Qs$.
Similarly, a declaration $\Ps_0.\f(\Ps)$ is \emph{more specific} than
a declaration $\Qs_0.\f(\Qs)$ if $(\Ps_0, \Ps) \morespecific (\Qs_0,
\Qs)$.

Now we describe how to determine which coercion is applied to a given
call in terms of rewriting functional calls.  The rewriting is
for pedagogical purposes; implementation techniques may vary.

Consider a static call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$.  Let $\Sigma$ be
the set of parameter types of functional declarations of $\f$ that are
applicable to the call.
Let $\Sigma'$ be the set of parameter types of
functional declarations of $\f$ that are
applicable with coercion to the call.
If $\Sigma$ is not empty then we use the overloading resolution
described in \secref{resolving-overloading} to determine which
element of $\Sigma$ is called.
If $\Sigma$ is empty but $\Sigma'$ is not, then we rewrite the call as
follows.  Define: \[\mathpzc{C} = \{T \in \Sigma' \mid S \coercedefto T
\logicand \As \Ovrsubtype S\}.\] Let $T \in \mathpzc{C}$ be the most
specific element of $\mathpzc{C}$.  In other words, there does not exist
$T' \in \mathpzc{C}$ such that $T' \morespecific T$.  The restrictions
given in \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} guarantee that such a $T$
exists and that it is unique.  The call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$ is
rewritten to \EXP{f(\mathrm{coercion}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(\TYP{A}))} or
\EXP{A_{0}.f(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(A))}
and the declaration with parameter
type $T$ is applied to the call.

As an example, consider the following definitions:
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}32 \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}64\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}128\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\\
\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = 1\)\\
\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}128) = 2\)
\end{Fortress}
Then the call \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}32)} resolves to the
declaration \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)} because $\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
\morespecific \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}$, which follows from the fact that
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.

Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is
statically chosen for a call, this coercion is conceptually inserted
into the call.
This means that the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time.

For example, in the following program:
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} A\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(c\COLONOP{}C) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} B \KWD{excludes} A \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} D \KWD{extends} \{B,C\} \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(f(a\COLONOP{}A) = 3\)\\
\(f(b\COLONOP{}B) = 4\)\\[4pt]
\(c \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} C = D\)\\
\(f(c)\)
\end{Fortress}
the call to \EXP{f(C)} resolves to the declaration
\EXP{f(A)} despite the fact that the declaration
\EXP{f(B)} is
applicable to the dynamic call \EXP{f(D)} and does not require
coercion.




\section{Restrictions on Coercion Declarations}
\seclabel{restrictions-coercion}

\end{Grammar}


Fortress supports what is sometimes called ``widest-need'' evaluation
of numerical expressions.  To see the problem, suppose that \VAR{a}
and \VAR{b} are 32-bit floating-point numbers and \VAR{c} is a 64-bit
floating-point number.  It is easy, and tempting, to write an
expression such as
\begin{Fortress}
\(c = c + a \cdot b\)
\end{Fortress}
but if you stop to think about it, if interpreted naively it will
compute the product \EXP{a \cdot b} as a 32-bit floating-point number,
and the impression that the sum may be accurate to the precision of a
64-bit floating-point number is only an illusion.  Widest-need
processing takes context into account and ``widens'' (or ``upgrades'')
the operands \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} to 64-bit floating-point numbers
before the product is computed, so that the product will be computed
as a 64-bit result.

Before widening is considered, a Fortress compiler,
in its normal course of operation, analyzes
an expression bottom-up.  For every functional invocation, it needs
to statically identify a specific declaration to be invoked.
Once this is done, then for %every argument position of
every functional invocation, one of two conditions holds:
(a) The type of the argument expression is a subtype of the
    type of the parameter in the identified declaration.
(b) The type of the argument expression can be coerced to the
    type of the parameter in the identified declaration.

This process has to be done bottom-up because in order to select a
specific declaration for a functional invocation, it is necessary to
know the types of the argument expressions, and if an argument
expression is itself a functional invocation, it is necessary to
select the specific declaration for that invocation in order to find
out the return type of the invocation.

Once an expression has been fully analyzed in this way, then widening
is performed as a top-down process.  For each functional invocation
that appears in a context where a coercion can occur, ask
whether the argument expression (which, remember, is a functional invocation)
falls under case (a) or case (b) above.  If case (b), coercion of the
functional result is required; if the relevant coercion declaration is
a ``widening'' coercion, then this functional invocation is a
candidate for widening.  Call the type of the functional invocation
\VAR{T}, and call the expected type of the coercion context, \VAR{U}.


When the functional call was considered during the bottom-up analysis,
in general many overloaded declarations may have been considered; of
all those that were applicable with coercion
to the static call, the most specific one was chosen.
When considering widening, we consider the same set of declarations, but
first discard all declarations whose return types are not subtypes of
\VAR{U}.  Then if any remain, and there is a unique most specific one
among them, then that declaration is attached to the functional call
instead.  In this way a coercion step is eliminated (coercion is no
longer needed to convert the result of the functional invocation from
type \VAR{T} to type \VAR{U}), possibly at the expense of requiring
a new coercion in a subexpression---but this is exactly the desired
effect.  Once this is done, then the subexpressions of the functional
call are processed recursively.


This process is general enough not only to provide for
widening floating-point precision, but to handle two other cases
of interest as well: widening point computations to interval computations,
and widening computations involving aggregate data structures whose
components are widenable.  For example, in \EXP{d (v \times w)} suppose that
\VAR{d} is of type $\mathbb{R}64$ and \VAR{v} and \VAR{w} are 3-vectors with components
of type $\mathbb{R}32$; this strategy is capable of promoting \VAR{v} and \VAR{w}
to 3-vectors with components of type $\mathbb{R}64$ and then performing all
computations with $\mathbb{R}64$ precision.

Let's go through the example of \EXP{c + a \cdot b} in detail.
The relevant declarations might look something like this:

\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{R}32\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{R}64\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(x\COLONOP\mathbb{R}32) \KWD{widens}\: = \ldots\)\\
\(  \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\cdot}(l\COLON \mathbb{R}32, r\COLON \mathbb{R}32)\COLON \mathbb{R}32 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  1 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\cdot}(l\COLON \mathbb{R}64, r\COLON \mathbb{R}64)\COLON \mathbb{R}64 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  2 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{opr} +(l\COLON \mathbb{R}32, r\COLON \mathbb{R}32)\COLON \mathbb{R}32 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  3 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{opr} +(l\COLON \mathbb{R}64, r\COLON \mathbb{R}64)\COLON \mathbb{R}64 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  4 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)
\end{Fortress}

The bottom-up analysis observes that \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} are both of type
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, and discovers that declarations \EXP{1} and \EXP{2}
are both applicable to the product, but declaration \EXP{1}
would be chosen because it requires no coercion and declaration \EXP{2}
would require coercion of both arguments to type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
The analysis then observes that \VAR{c} has type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
and the product expression has type \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, so declaration
\EXP{3} is not applicable but declaration \EXP{4} is applicable
(though requiring a coercion from \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} for its second argument).

Now the top-down widening analysis is performed.  The product is
a functional call that is an argument to another functional call,
and its result requires coercion, and that coercion is a widening
coercion.  Therefore the compiler reconsiders the applicable
declarations, which were declarations \EXP{1} and \EXP{2}.
The result type of declaration \EXP{1} is not a subtype
of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, but the result type of declaration \EXP{2}
is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (in fact, it \emph{is} \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}).
Declaration \EXP{2} is the most specific among the applicable declarations
with that property (in fact, in this example it's the only one),
so declaration \EXP{2} replaces declaration \EXP{1} for the
product invocation.  This in turn requires \VAR{a} and \VAR{b}
to be coerced from type \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
before the product is performed.

Widening is a tricky business, best left to expert library designers.
When used judiciously, it can greatly improve the precision of
numerical computations without requiring a great deal of thought on
the part of the application programmer and without cluttering up code
with explicit conversions.


\emph{Future versions of this specification will include tables of
  coercions and widening coercions supported by \library.}

% the generic type defined by the trait declaration 
% is \emph{covariant} in that parameter.
% Victor: I had the above text,
% but it was convenient to define "covariant parameter":
it is a \emph{covariant parameter} 
of the generic type defined by the trait declaration.
% Victor: the following sentence is a bit unwieldy.
One instantiation of a generic type 
is a subtype of another instantiation of the same generic type 
if the argument instantiating each covariant parameter 
in the first instantiation 
is a subtype of the corresponding argument 
in the second instantiation, 
and the argument instantiating each non-covariant parameter 
is the same in both instantiations.

Every trait type excludes \Void, \Bottom\ and every tuple type.
Every trait type other than \Object\ 
also excludes every arrow type and function type.
A trait declaration may have an \KWD{excludes} clause, 
which also specifies a set of types and 
generic types determined by the generic type defined by the declaration.
% Victor: Do we have a term for this set?
%   Perhaps it should be defined in the traits chapter.
An instantiation of the generic type defined by such a declaration 
excludes every type in this set 
and the corresponding instantiation of each generic type in this set.

% Multiple instantiation exclusion
% Victor: I've shortened this to instantiation exclusion.
Fortress also imposes a rule called \emph{instantiation exclusion}:
% which defines the exclusion relation for different instantiations of a generic type:
Two instantiations of a generic trait type exclude each other 
if the corresponding arguments for any covariant parameter exclude each other, 
or if the corresponding arguments for any non-covariant parameter 
are not type equivalent.
\note{I believe this exactly characterizes exclusion
among different instantiations of a generic type, 
but the rule we impose is stronger:
Any trait that extends (possibly indirectly) 
two instantiations of a generic type 
must extend an \emph{expressible} instantiation of that generic type 
that is a subtype of both.
In other words,
among all instantiations of a generic type 
that are supertypes of some expressible trait type, 
one must be a subtype of all the others, 
and it must be expressible.
This section should say only which instantiations exclude each other,
as it does.
It perhaps should make it clearer that what is said here 
is a consequence of instantiation exclusion, 
which is a rule applied to trait declarations.}


% An object trait type is a leaf type:
An object trait type has no strict subtype other than \Bottom, 
and it excludes any type that is not its supertype.

A trait declaration may have a \KWD{comprises} clause, 
which also specifies a set of types and 
generic types determined by the generic type of the declaration.
An instantiation of the generic type defined by such a declaration 
is covered by the union 
of the types in this set 
and the corresponding instantiations of the generic type in this set.

% Victor: I'm not sure about the proper terminology here.
A trait or object declaration may provide a \emph{coercion} from a type or a generic type.
(See \secref{coercion-decl} and \chapref{coercion}.)
If a trait or object declaration provides a coercion from a type, 
then any instantiation of the generic type defined by that declaration 
coerces that type.
If it provides a coercion from a generic type, 
then an instantiation of the generic type defined by that declaration 
coerces the corresponding instantiation of the generic type of the coercion.

\section{Types in the Fortress Standard Libraries}
\seclabel{types-libraries}

\Library\ define simple standard types for literals such as
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket{}b\rrbracket},
\TYP{()} (pronounced ``void''),
\TYP{Character}, \TYP{String}, and
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{b}, \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}
(See \secref{literals} for a discussion of Fortress literals).
Moreover, there are several simple standard numeric types.
These types are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them.
Values of these types are immutable.

The numeric types share the common supertype \TYP{Number}.
Fortress includes types for
arbitrary-precision integers (of type $\mathbb{Z}$),
their unsigned equivalents (of type $\mathbb{N}$),
rational numbers (of type $\mathbb{Q}$),
real numbers (of type $\mathbb{R}$),
complex numbers (of type $\mathbb{C}$),
fixed-size representations for integers including the types
{$\mathbb{Z}$8}, {$\mathbb{Z}$16}, {$\mathbb{Z}$32}, {$\mathbb{Z}$64},
{$\mathbb{Z}$128}, their unsigned equivalents
{$\mathbb{N}$8}, {$\mathbb{N}$16}, {$\mathbb{N}$32}, {$\mathbb{N}$64},
{$\mathbb{N}$128},
floating-point numbers (described below),
intervals (of type \EXP{\TYP{Interval}\bTPl X\bTPr},
abbreviated as \EXP{\bsINT{X}},
where \EXP{X} can be instantiated
with any number type), and imaginary and complex numbers of fixed size
(in rectangular form with types $\mathbb{C}n$ for $n = 16, 32, 64, 128, 256$
and polar form with type \EXP{\TYP{Polar}\bsTP{X}} where \EXP{X} can
be instantiated with any real number type).

\Library\ also define other simple standard types such as \TYP{Any},
\TYP{Object}, \TYP{Exception}, \TYP{Boolean}, and \TYP{BooleanInterval}
as well as low-level binary data types such as \TYP{LinearSequence},
\TYP{HeapSequence}, and \TYP{BinaryWord}.
See Parts~\ref{part:basic-lib} and \ref{part:advanced-lib} for discussions
of \library.


\section{Intersection and Union Types}
\seclabel{internal-types}

For every finite set of types, there is a type denoting a unique
\emph{intersection} of those types.
The intersection of a set of types $S$ is a subtype of every type $T \in S$
and of the intersection of every subset of $S$.

    16	The trait \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}star}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} with
    17	two extra elements, \EXP{+\infty} and \EXP{-\infty}.
    18	
    19	Often it is desirable to indicate that a variable ranges over only a subset of
    20	the integers, such as only positive values or only nonnegative values or only
    21	nonzero values.
    22	Fortress uses a system similar to that for rational numbers, but also
    23	accommodates the traditional use of \EXP{\mathbb{N}} to denote the natural numbers:
    24	
    25	\begin{tabbing}
    26	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} (\STR{ZZ}) is the set of integers
    27	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*}).
    28	\\
    29	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{<}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}LT}) is the set of strictly negative integers
    30	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\neq}}).
    31	\\
    32	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\leq}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}LE}) is the set of nonpositive integers, that is, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{<} \cup \{0\}}
    33	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\leq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}).
    34	\\
    35	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}GE}) is the set of nonnegative integers, that is, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{>} \cup \{0\}}
    36	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\geq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}).
    37	\\
    38	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{>}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}GT}) is the set of strictly positive integers
    39	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\neq}}).
    40	\\
    41	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\neq}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}NE}) is the set of strictly nonzero integers (that is, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{<} \cup \mathbb{Z}_{>}})
    42	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\neq}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\neq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}).
    43	\\
    44	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}star}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} with extra elements \EXP{+\infty} and \EXP{-\infty}
    45	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}).
    46	\\
    47	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{<}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}star{\char'137}LT}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{<}} with extra element \EXP{-\infty}
    48	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{<}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\leq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\neq}}).
    49	\\
    50	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\leq}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}star{\char'137}LE}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\leq}} with extra element \EXP{-\infty}
    51	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\leq}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*}).
    52	\\
    53	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\geq}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}star{\char'137}GE}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}} with extra element \EXP{+\infty}
    54	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\geq}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*}).
    55	\\
    56	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{>}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}star{\char'137}GT}) is \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{>}} with extra element \EXP{+\infty}
    57	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{>}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\geq}}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\neq}}).
    58	\\
    59	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*_{\neq}} (\STR{ZZ{\char'137}star{\char'137}NE}) is
    60	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\neq}} with extra elements \EXP{+\infty} and \EXP{-\infty}
    61	(it is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*_{\neq}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Z}^*}).
    62	\\
    63	\EXP{\mathbb{N}} (\STR{NN}) is a synonym for \EXP{\mathbb{Z}_{\geq}}.

Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations

in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.

18: The standard types for rational numbers such as \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}
19: and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}_{\leq}} are defined in terms of a single trait \TYP{RationalQuantity}
20: that handles dimensions and units as well as performing a case analysis to distinguish
21: rather a particular expression is guaranteed not to produce infinities, \EXP{0/0},
22: or numbers of a particular sign.
23: 
24: The trait \TYP{RationalQuantity} takes seven static parameters; the first is a dimensional unit,
25: and the others are booleans specifying whether an instance of the trait can possibly
26: be \EXP{-\infty}, a finite rational less than zero, zero, a finite rational greater than zero,
27: \EXP{+\infty}, or \EXP{0/0}.  This allows the standard rational types to be represented

******************************************************************************)

component conditionalExtension

export Executable

trait PartialOrderAndBoundedLattice[\T, opr LEOPR, opr MINOPR, opr MAXOPR\] end
trait Identity[\opr PLUS\] end

trait RationalQuantity[\unit U absorbs unit, bool ninf, bool lt, bool eq,
                        bool gt, bool pinf, bool nan\]
    extends {
      RationalQuantity[\U, ninf', lt', eq', gt', pinf', nan'\]
              where [\bool ninf', bool lt', bool eq', bool gt', bool pinf',
                      bool nan' \]
                    { ninf IMPLIES ninf', lt IMPLIES lt',
                      eq IMPLIES eq', gt IMPLIES gt', pinf IMPLIES pinf',
                      nan IMPLIES nan'
                    },
              PartialOrderAndBoundedLattice[\RationalQuantity[\U, ninf, lt, eq, gt, pinf, nan\], <=, MIN, MAX\]
              where { ninf AND pinf AND NOT nan }
            }
    where { ninf OR lt OR eq OR gt OR pinf OR nan }
  coerce(x: Identity[\+\]) = 0
end

run() = println "Conditional extension with where clauses can be parsed."

end

(* Q3RefineWalk -- does the RationalQuantity design run on the interpreter?
   A trait with bool static parameters whose extends clause names other
   instantiations of itself under a where clause (numbers-advanced.tex:261-290,
   ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss), a type alias for one
   instantiation (numbers-advanced.tex:47-66), and a call that needs the
   conditional subtyping: a strictly positive value passed where a
   nonnegative one is expected. *)
component Q3RefineWalk
export Executable

trait RQ[\bool lt, bool eq, bool gt\]
    extends { RQ[\lt', eq', gt'\]
              where [\bool lt', bool eq', bool gt'\]
                    { lt IMPLIES lt', eq IMPLIES eq', gt IMPLIES gt' } }
    where { lt OR eq OR gt }
    v(): ZZ32
end

object Pos(x: ZZ32) extends RQ[\false,false,true\]
    v(): ZZ32 = x
end

(* QQ_GE's shape: a parameter that admits zero and the positives *)
nonneg(q: RQ[\false,true,true\]): ZZ32 = q.v()

run(): () = do
    p = Pos(3)
    println("Pos(3) built: " p.v())
    println("instanceof RQ[\\false,false,true\\]: " (p ISA RQ[\false,false,true\]))
    println("instanceof RQ[\\false,true,true\\] (the conditional supertype): " (p ISA RQ[\false,true,true\]))
    println("nonneg(Pos(3)) = " nonneg(p))
  end
end
EOF

(* Q3RefineWalk -- does the RationalQuantity design run on the interpreter?
   A trait with bool static parameters whose extends clause names other
   instantiations of itself under a where clause (numbers-advanced.tex:261-290;
   the team's ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss only parses it),
   and a call that needs the conditional subtyping: a strictly positive value
   passed where a nonnegative one is expected (QQ_GT where QQ_GE is asked).
   (The trait is Rat, not RQ: a word of two or more capitals is an operator.
   A bool static argument list is written with a space after each comma:
   Rat[\false,true\] in a parameter type is a syntax error on this tree,
   Rat[\false, true\] parses.) *)
component Q3RefineWalk
export Executable

trait Rat[\bool lt, bool eq, bool gt\]
    extends { Rat[\lt', eq', gt'\]
              where [\bool lt', bool eq', bool gt'\]
                    { lt IMPLIES lt', eq IMPLIES eq', gt IMPLIES gt' } }
    where { lt OR eq OR gt }
    v(): ZZ32
end

object Pos(x: ZZ32) extends Rat[\false, false, true\]
    v(): ZZ32 = x
end

(* QQ_GT's shape and QQ_GE's shape as parameter types *)
positive(q: Rat[\false, false, true\]): ZZ32 = q.v()
nonneg(q: Rat[\false, true, true\]): ZZ32 = q.v()

run(): () = do
    p = Pos(3)
    println("positive(Pos(3)) = " positive(p))
    println("nonneg(Pos(3)), which needs Rat[\\false, false, true\\] <: Rat[\\false, true, true\\]:")
    println("  = " nonneg(p))
  end
end
EOF
cd /home/user/fortress; SCRATCH=/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad explorations/reviews/flattening-questions-ways/walk.sh Q3RefineWalk 2>&1 | head -20

(* Q2WidthWalk -- mixed widths on the interpreter today: a ZZ32 beside a ZZ64
   in arithmetic, in a range lo:hi and lo#n, and in a generic call's inferred
   static argument; a variable declared ZZ64 that holds a 32-bit number; and
   the real-by-integer mixtures the two microGPT programs write.  Each line is
   the value and its run-time type (ilkName). *)
component Q2WidthWalk
export Executable

show(tag: String, x: Object): () = println(tag ": " x " : " x.ilkName)

(* a generic call whose static argument is inferred from two arguments *)
pair[\T\](x: T, y: T): Array[\T,ZZ32\] = do
    p = array[\T\](2)
    p[0] := x
    p[1] := y
    p
  end
(* ProjectFortress/demos/fact64.fss:28, called without its widen *)
fact(x: ZZ64): ZZ64 = if x < 2 then 1 else x fact(x - 1) end

run(): () = do
    a: ZZ32 = 2147483647
    b: ZZ64 = 1                 (* declared ZZ64, holds a 32-bit number *)
    c: ZZ64 = widen(1)          (* a 64-bit number *)
    show("b: ZZ64 = 1", b)
    show("c: ZZ64 = widen(1)", c)
    show("a + b   (a: ZZ32 = 2^31-1)", a + b)
    show("a + c", a + c)
    show("b + a", b + a)
    m: ZZ64 = 100000
    show("m: ZZ64 = 100000; m m", m m)
    n: ZZ64 = widen(100000)
    show("n: ZZ64 = widen(100000); n n", n n)
    h: ZZ64 = 3000000000
    show("h: ZZ64 = 3000000000", h)
    show("a + h", a + h)
    z: ZZ64 = 0
    show("z: ZZ64 = 0; z.maximum   (longPrim.fss shape)", z.maximum)
    show("widen(0).maximum", (widen(0)).maximum)
    show("fact(20), x: ZZ64 given the literal 20", fact(20))
    show("fact(widen(20))", fact(widen(20)))
    (* ranges with one end of each width *)
    show("0 : c   (ZZ32 : ZZ64)", 0 : c)
    show("0 # c   (ZZ32 # ZZ64)", 0 # c)
    show("a : (widen(a) + 2), elements", <| i | i <- seq(a : (widen(a) + 2)) |>)
    show("first element's type", (<| i | i <- seq(a : (widen(a) + 2)) |>)[0])
    (* the inferred static argument of a generic call *)
    show("pair(a, c)   (ZZ32, ZZ64)", pair(a, c))
    show("pair(c, a)   (ZZ64, ZZ32)", pair(c, a))
    show("pair(a, 0.5) (ZZ32, RR64)", pair(a, 0.5))
    (* the real-by-integer mixtures of MicroGptFlat.fss *)
    s: ZZ32 = 3
    show("1.0 s   (MicroGptFlat.fss:82)", 1.0 s)
    show("(1.0 s) / 1000   (ZZ32 divisor)", (1.0 s) / 1000)
    show("1 - 0.85   (MicroGptFlat.fss:77)", 1 - 0.85)
    show("2 (10.0^(-6))   (MicroGptFlatCheck.fss:86)", 2 (10.0^(-6)))
    show("10.0^(-5)   (MicroGptFlat.fss:18)", 10.0^(-5))
    show("0.85^s   (MicroGptFlat.fss:79)", 0.85^s)
    show("10.0 (0.5) + (57 - 48)   (FlatData.fss:26)", 10.0 (0.5) + (57 - 48))
    t0 = nanoTime()
    show("nanoTime()", t0)
    show("(nanoTime() - t0) DIV 1000000", (nanoTime() - t0) DIV 1000000)
    x = array[\RR64\](4).fill(0.5)
    show("(x DOT x) / |x|   (MicroGptFlat.fss:27)", (x DOT x) / |x|)
  end
end

content.content:
1c492019f 2007-12-13 jmaessen
Fiddled with reductions (particularly Sum reduction) in effort to get
something we can desugar to (but this required a bit of kludging on
the type side: the declarations are correct but don't yield as
specific type information as one would like).

Built first cut at FortressLibrary.fsi.  This is untested, but is
something we can work against in revising the linking phase.

fca589bbb 2008-07-15 jmaessen
IntLiteral is now a subtype of ZZ32 (and thus of every other numeric
type).  But there are a number of caveats:
* ZZ32 is now a trait, with subtypes Int and IntLiteral.  In practice
all the ZZ32 math you do will end up yielding results of type Int.
This means that when you stuff the results into a polymorphically-typed
container (such as Maybe or List) the type variable will invariably be
dynamically instantiated with Int, rather than ZZ32 as you'd expect.
Most of the changes in this checkin address this in the regression
tests.
* In order to obtain the expected behavior with large constants,
evaluation a too-large IntLiteral actually yields a ZZ.  This means in
practice that the interpreter never actually creates an object of type
IntLiteral.  The reason this is necessary is because we will otherwise
attempt to use ZZ32 arithmetic on any constant that is too big to fit
in ZZ64!  You might imagine an alternative workaround where we define
redundant math on IntLiterals that yields ZZ, but this will cause all
kinds of problems with the overloading rules as it violates
subtyping.  In practice programmers shouldn't notice this at all (in
stark, stark contrast to the previous bullet).
* A couple of test were invalidated.  XXXextendZZ32.fss doesn't spot
its failure condition (extending a closed trait); it was previously
extending a closed object type and failed as expected.  This has been
filed as a bug.
SpecData/examples/basic/StatPara.Opr.IDENTITYplus.fss appears to have
been fundamentally wrong all along, and we suddenly started spotting
and reporting the bug.  It's been deleted as it was unused in the spec.

In the example above,
if `String` and `ZZ` exclude each other,\!\footnote{
Indeed, `String` and `ZZ` \emph{are} declared to exclude
each other in the Fortress standard library.}
then the overloaded definitions of `print` above are valid.

We already exploited exclusion 
in our prior work on Fortress without generics, 
but the constructs Fortress provides for explicitly declaring exclusion 
are insufficient for allowing 
some intuitively appealing overloaded functions involving generic types.
In particular, 
we could not guarantee type safety 
when a type extends multiple instantiations of a generic type.
Implicitly forbidding such extension---%
a property we call \emph{multiple instantiation exclusion}---%
allows these intuitively appealing overloaded functions.
